event.title: Nepal flash flood, Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor

location.region: Langtang Lirung / Lhende–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor (Rasuwa and downstream)

event.summary: On 26 August 2026, ice and rock broke from Langtang Lirung on the Nepal-China border. Within minutes the surge became a debris flood. It then raced down the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli rivers. Towns, farms, and power plants were destroyed. Thousands of people were killed or left missing.
event.hero: A wall of ice and rock let go above a river in Nepal.

nodes.title: The Himalaya is warming because of us
nodes.description: Human greenhouse gases trapped extra heat in the high Himalaya. A World Weather Attribution study found the July-August warmth around the failure site was about 1.5°C hotter than a pre-industrial climate would have been. That extra heat sits on a longer warming trend. Glaciers thin. Frozen ground thaws. Ice that once glued rock fractures together weakens. Climate change is a destabilising factor on a slope that already had geological weaknesses. It is not the sole cause of the collapse.

nodes.title: Ice and frozen ground were already loosening the slope
nodes.description: Glaciers in the region have been thinning by more than half a metre of ice-equivalent a year. Permafrost thaw and a rising rain-snow line weaken ice-bonded fractures in the rock. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake may also have loosened the slope. Its specific role in the 2026 failure is not confirmed.

nodes.title: A slab of mountain broke free
nodes.description: On 26 August 2026 at about 08:37 NPT, roughly 2 km² of rock wall and glacier ice failed on Langtang Lirung, around 5,150 m. The mass fell about 1,400 m. It produced seismic waves first mistaken for an earthquake. It slammed into the Lhende catchment and became a debris flood.

nodes.title: The fall became a wall of mud, rock, and water
nodes.description: The avalanche turned into a debris flood in the Lhende catchment. Early reconstructions put the surge at Rasuwagadhi in about seven minutes. A brief river choke of minutes is possible. A long-lived dam burst is not what the arrival timing shows.

nodes.title: A flash flood tore down the river corridor
nodes.description: The surge reached the Nepal-China border in minutes. It kept destroying towns, bridges, and power sites far down the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli system. World Weather Attribution, citing government and UNDP figures, reports over 1,300 confirmed deaths in Nepal. Over 5,000 people were missing. About 84,270 people were affected across six districts.

nodes.title: Power plants went dark and farms were buried
nodes.description: UNDP’s preliminary RAPIDA assessment estimated at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris in analysed areas. Eleven hydropower stations and one solar plant totalling 431.1 MW stopped operating. About 10,451 people had been rescued by 1 September. Debris buried buildings and fields. Rescue work ran for days.

nodes.title: Rice and other crops were wiped out
nodes.description: FAO’s preliminary assessment found about 1,800 hectares of crops damaged, mostly paddy. Production losses approached 7,700 tonnes. Livestock, fishponds, food stocks, and farm infrastructure were also hit. Restoring land, irrigation, and seeds before the next planting season is the immediate agricultural task.

nodes.title: Farming families lost more than one harvest
nodes.description: When fields, animals, and food stocks go at once, household income and food security take longer to recover than the flood itself. FAO says farming families face that longer squeeze even after the water recedes. Household-level income losses for this event are not yet fully quantified.

nodes.title: Wider economic fallout is still unproven
nodes.description: National GDP or market-wide losses from this specific flood have not been established in a verified primary assessment. Documented damage to power, crops, and homes is already large. The next economic layer is still being counted. We do not yet have evidence either way for a national total.

claims.text: A study measured how much extra heat climate change added. Human-caused warming made the July-August warmth at and around the failure site about 1.5°C hotter than a pre-industrial baseline would have. That extra heat sits on a longer Himalayan warming trend that thins glaciers and degrades permafrost.
claims.caveat: Climate change is described as a destabilising factor on a pre-existing geological predisposition, not the sole or fundamental cause of the slope failure.

claims.text: Glaciers in the region have been thinning by more than half a metre of ice-equivalent a year. Permafrost thaw and a rising rain-snow line likely weakened ice-bonded fractures before the collapse. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake may also have preconditioned the slope. Its specific contribution to the 2026 failure is not confirmed.
claims.methodology_status: expert synthesis; not a single-event binary attribution
claims.caveat: WWA did not assess whether this specific avalanche would have occurred without human-induced warming.

claims.text: On 26 August 2026 at about 08:37 NPT, roughly 2 km² of rock wall and glacier ice failed on Langtang Lirung, around 5,150 m. The mass fell about 1,400 m. It produced seismic waves first mistaken for an earthquake. The flow entered the Lhende catchment and became a debris flood.
claims.methodology_status: multi-source observational reconstruction (seismic + satellite + field reports)

claims.text: The debris flood reached Rasuwagadhi within about seven minutes. Early reconstructions put the average speed near 188 km/h. HiRisk notes the Lhende Khola may have been dammed only for minutes. Independent open-data work finds a sustained dam-and-breach sequence inconsistent with arrival timing.
claims.methodology_status: observed impacts; mechanism details still refining
claims.caveat: Do not treat a long-lived barrier-lake breach as established for the initial surge; secondary upstream lakes were reported in following days as a separate concern.

claims.text: UNDP’s preliminary RAPIDA assessment estimated at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris in analysed areas. About 556,200 tonnes of that came from building debris across 2,359 assessed buildings. Eleven hydropower stations and one solar plant totalling 431.1 MW stopped operating. Fifteen projects under construction, totalling 470 MW planned, were also damaged. About 10,451 people had been rescued by 1 September. World Weather Attribution, citing government and UNDP figures as of mid-September, reports over 1,300 confirmed deaths in Nepal. Over 5,000 people were missing. An estimated 84,270 people were affected across six districts.
claims.geographic_scope: Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor; Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, Tanahu
claims.methodology_status: preliminary, satellite damage mapping + engineering estimates; figures may rise
claims.caveat: Debris and casualty figures are preliminary and were still being updated after publication.

claims.text: FAO’s preliminary assessment found about 1,800 hectares of crops damaged, mostly paddy. Production losses approached 7,700 tonnes. Livestock, farmland, fisheries, food stocks, and agricultural infrastructure were also hit.
claims.geographic_scope: Affected agricultural areas along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor
claims.caveat: A later national RDNA (NPC/NDRRMA), as reported in Nepali media, gave more granular paddy figures (e.g. 1,669 ha / 5,843 tonnes rice; ~NPR 1.09 billion crop losses). Those RDNA numbers are not yet tied here to a retrieved primary PDF, see internal note in sources.

claims.text: This is a reasonable link, but no study has confirmed household income losses for this specific event yet. FAO stated that damage to crops, livestock, fishponds, food stocks, and farm infrastructure threatens food security well beyond the immediate emergency. Restoring farmland, irrigation, seeds, and veterinary support before the next planting season is critical.
claims.methodology_status: institutional qualitative assessment grounded in observed agricultural damage
claims.caveat: Household-level income and food-security outcomes for this specific event are not yet fully quantified in the sources used here.

timeline.label: Flash flood occurs
timeline.detail: On 26 August 2026 at about 08:37 NPT, the Langtang Lirung rock-ice collapse began. The debris flood reached Rasuwagadhi within minutes.

timeline.label: Infrastructure disruption
timeline.detail: Hydropower stations totalling 431.1 MW went offline, according to UNDP. Search and rescue continued under debris and blocked roads.

timeline.label: Damage assessments published
timeline.detail: UNDP published RAPIDA debris and energy figures on 1 September. FAO published its agricultural assessment around 10 September. World Weather Attribution published its climate-hazard synthesis on 17 September.

timeline.label: Supply-chain / local economy
timeline.detail: A verified primary macroeconomic assessment for this flood is not yet available.

timeline.label: Long-term ecosystem / recovery
timeline.detail: Recovery and ecosystem trajectories remain open questions. We do not yet have evidence either way.

what_we_know: A rock-ice avalanche on Langtang Lirung on 26 August 2026 triggered a debris flood down the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor.
Human-caused warming made the surrounding season about 1.5°C hotter. Scientists treat that extra heat as a contributing factor alongside geology, not the sole cause.
Preliminary assessments document major debris volumes, hydropower outages, crop damage, and large humanitarian impacts.
what_remains_uncertain: Whether a short-lived river choke lasted only minutes, versus a purely continuous debris-flood pulse.
Whether this exact avalanche would have occurred without human-induced warming.
Household livelihood outcomes and broader economic effects beyond documented damage.
Final death, missing, and debris totals, which were still being revised.
